transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 09:00 PT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Sara (Lunaris), Rajiv (Lunaris Infra), Emily (Lunaris Data)

Summary: Cost/unit econ deep dive for POC; benchmarks and tuning.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): ok, hi everyone, thanks for joining, we have about 45 minutes, quick agenda — benchmark review, caching, batching tradeoffs, next steps. Uh feel free to jump in.
[00:21] Sara (Lunaris): thanks Maya, yeah we're excited to see where the numbers landed this week. we ran your last suggested run and saw some differences.
[00:35] Daniel (Redwood): cool, i'll start with the high-level numbers, then we can dig in. so top line: tokens per second and tokens per dollar — we measured across three profiles: small batch (1-4), medium (8-12) and large (16-32).
[00:50] Daniel (Redwood): in the medium profile we saw ~2,100 tokens/sec on the A100-style instance and tokens per dollar around 45k tokens per $1, but this is with fp16 and no kv-cash- sorry kv-cache.
[01:10] Rajiv (Lunaris): wait 45k tokens per dollar, can you repeat that, because our earlier run with Vertex AI looked like 30k.
[01:20] Daniel: yeah so for redwoods hosted runtime with the batching we configured, the efficiency bump is visible. the numbers vary with seq length distribution — for your prod-like dataset where median seq len is 64, the effective tokens/$ is higher.
[01:35] Emily (Lunaris): small quibble: in our test we have a fat tail out to 512 tokens on 5% of requests, does that skew the metric?
[01:47] Daniel: it does; the tail increases per-token compute and reduces tokens/sec and tokens per dollar. we try to normalize by weighting by your traffic percentiles.
[02:00] Maya: maybe worth clarifying: when we say tokens per dollar we're combining throughput, GPU utilization, and model size + quantization delta. so the 45k number is for the curated model+quant profile we used. with int8-ish quant we saw another ~20% cost improvement but some regen quality delta.
[02:20] Sara: that's the tradeoff — we can't lose generation quality; our SLAs for summary coherence are strict.
[02:30] Daniel: understood. we can run a regen-quality A/B on a held prompt set — that's in the deck.
[02:40] Maya: back to caching — last week you asked about prefix caching vs KV cache, we ran both. daniel?
[02:48] Daniel: yes. small note, transcription earlier had the term 'KV cash' in our notes, it's KV cache. so prefix cache gave about 12% token savings across the board but kv-cache with a tuned prefix hit rate gave ~33% token saving for your conversational workflow where prefix repeats are common.
[03:10] Rajiv: 33% is big. what was the hit rate distribution?
[03:16] Daniel: median hit rate around 0.28, 75th percentile 0.6, but that depends on the exact prefix length threshold we set. the effective saving maps roughly: tokens_saved = hit_rate * avg_prefix_len.
[03:30] Emily: and that was on the model variant with kv enabled, any extra memory overhead?
[03:35] Daniel: yes, KV uses additional memory per request; on our benchmark harness it increased GPU memory by ~8% which is fine on dedicated capacity but matters for small hosted nodes.
[03:48] Sara: so is the plan to enable KV-cache in prod? we have concerns about session stickiness and routing.
[03:55] Maya: right, KV-cache requires some routing considerations — we can do sticky routing at the service level or fall back to session affinity. that has impact on autoscaling and cost.
[04:08] Rajiv: how about failover? if a node that has the cache goes down, do we lose the cache and pay regen cost?
[04:15] Daniel: yes, that's why we recommend a hybrid — keep small TTL and use fallback model variants to reduce cold-start penalty; Redwood's runtime supports automatic fallback to a compatible variant.
[04:30] Sara: ok noted.
[04:35] Maya: batching — we saw diminishing returns past batch 16 for your workload. daniel you have the numbers?
[04:42] Daniel: sure, batch 1-4: tokens/sec ~650, median latency 120ms per token; batch 8-12: tokens/sec ~1,900, latency increases but still within your 95th of 500ms; batch 16-32: tokens/sec ~2,400 but 95th latency approaches 900ms which fails your SLO. so cost-wise it's best at 8-12 given your latency target.
[05:10] Rajiv: is that tokens/sec measured per-GPU or cluster-level?
[05:14] Daniel: per-GPU in the bench harness. cluster-level you multiply by the number of GPUs but you also need to account for packing efficiency.
[05:22] Emily: what about concurrency? we have bursts up to 500 reqs/sec. will batching help or hurt for spikes?
[05:30] Daniel: batching helps smooth spikes but if bursts are too short it won't hit large batch sizes; we recommend a hybrid auto-batcher with small latency budget and burst capacity to fall back to dedicated spare capacity for peak.
[05:44] Maya: and we showed the cost math in the sheet — tokens/sec/$ column normalizes across those configs. link again: https://redwood.app/sheets/lunaris-poc-costs (shared).
[05:55] Sara: got it, will review.
[06:00] Daniel: another point — quantization. fp16 is baseline, int8-ish gives ~20-30% better tokens/$, but regen quality can shift on your prompt set; we should run the quality regression tests before switching.
[06:16] Rajiv: can you run int8 profile with caching and batching? that compound effect might give large cost wins.
[06:22] Daniel: yes we can. we expect marginal returns stacking — caching reduces tokens charged, quantization lowers per-token compute. stacked you might see 40-45% cost reduction vs baseline but need regen checks.
[06:40] Emily: do you have guidance on hosted vs dedicated? we were leaning dedicated for compliance but cost math was fuzzy.
[06:48] Maya: dedicated gives you better predictability and allows larger models/kv caches without noisy neighbor issues. Hosted is easier to start and has burst options. For unit economics, dedicated tends to win at sustained high QPS because utilization is under your control.
[07:05] Sara: what's the break-even QPS for dedicated?
[07:09] Daniel: rough rule: if sustained effective tokens/sec needed exceeds ~150k tokens/sec for a month, dedicated typically beats hosted on tokens/$, but this depends on model size, reserved instance pricing and your commit level. we'll model that explicitly in the sheet.
[07:25] Rajiv: ok, please add our current forecast to that calc.
[07:30] Maya: yes, action item: Rajiv to share traffic distribution.
[07:36] Speaker 1 (unknown): uh quick question on encryption — does kv-cache persist anything to disk?
[07:42] Daniel: no persistent disk for the KV in our default config, it's in-memory on the node, but we support encrypted snapshots and KMS integration if you want persistence with HSM-backed keys.
[07:55] Emily: good, will put that in security review.
[08:00] Sara: can we talk about the new run you uploaded? the tokens/$ seemed better but the latency percentiles were different.
[08:08] Daniel: that run enabled adaptive batching and a slightly different packing policy; that improved average tokens/sec but tail latency increased. we can tune aggressiveness to meet your 95th bound.
[08:25] Sara: do we have concrete numbers for cost delta with KV-cache enabled?
[08:29] Daniel: with your sample dataset, enabling kv-cache decreased billed tokens by ~32% and overall tokens/$ improved by ~28% after accounting for the memory overhead.
[08:40] Rajiv: how confident are you that the 32% will generalize?
[08:45] Daniel: confidence is medium — it depends on prefix reuse. we suggested running a longer 24-hour capture to confirm hit-rate stability.
[08:56] Emily: we can run that this week.
[09:00] Maya: perfect. next, on the topic of routing and autoscaling: sticky routing for cache requires slightly different autoscaler thresholds. it can raise cost for small workloads due to underpacking; we can simulate that.
[09:18] Rajiv: will this complicate a multi-region failover?
[09:22] Daniel: a bit; either you accept some cache cold starts for cross-region failover or you replicate cache states which increases cost. for most customers we prefer ephemeral per-region caching + short TTLs.
[09:36] Sara: makes sense.
[09:40] Maya: timeline — next week we'll run the two batch profiles Daniel suggested, plus kv-cache 24-hour run, and update the sheet. follow-up on 2026-03-11.
[09:52] Daniel: i'll note the exact batch configs: small (1-4), medium (8-12), and large (16-32) and will instrument request-level traces for tail latency.
[10:03] Emily: can you also add a column for tokens/sec per GPU and per-dollar normalized to our commit price?
[10:09] Maya: yes we'll normalize to your projected reserved prices in the sheet.
[10:15] Sara: any legal or procurement blockers for dedicated if we decide to move?
[10:20] Maya: you'd need a standard enterprise contract and typical SOC2 + SAML SSO integrations; we can have legal start a draft once you signal intent.
[10:30] Rajiv: security-wise, we need KMS/HSM alignments; you mentioned support?
[10:34] Daniel: yes, we support cloud KMS and bring-your-own HSM via the private deployment option.
[10:40] Speaker 2 (internal): small note — someone in engineering reported a mismatch in the perf harness naming (A100 vs A40) in the last doc, fix that.
[10:48] Daniel: thanks, we'll correct the hardware labels.
[10:52] Maya: wrapping up, quick recap: runs to do (batch profiles + kv 24h + int8 run with caching), Rajiv to provide traffic distribution and security requirements, Maya to share updated cost model + annotated sheet, follow-up 2026-03-11.
[11:10] Sara: thanks everyone, that covers it.
[11:15] Rajiv: thanks, bye.
[11:18] Maya: bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hear of 'kv-cache' as 'kv-cash' in auto notes; speaker tags approximate.

Attachments / shared links: https://redwood.app/sheets/lunaris-poc-costs (benchmarks), https://redwood.app/docs/poc-checklist, sample traces uploaded to shared drive (link in sheet).

End of transcript.
